extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; policymakers and historians interested in democracy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Tocqueville's normative claims about democracy, religion, labor, manufactures, and manners as actionable principles or evaluative standards. Useful for applying his prescriptions to analysis of democratic societies or policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of materialism in democratic peoples
rubrics_metrics.description: Materialism is, amongst all nations, a dangerous disease of the human mind; but it is more especially to be dreaded amongst a democratic people, because it readily amalgamates with that vice which is most familiar to the heart under such circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains causal link: democracy encourages a taste for physical gratification which predisposes men to materialism; materialism then intensifies appetite for bodily pleasures, producing a vicious cycle that brutalizes society. The passage warns governments and moralists to see the danger and restrain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religions teach immortality and should be preserved in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Most religions are only general, simple, and practical means of teaching men the doctrine of the immortality of the soul. That is the greatest benefit which a democratic people derives, from its belief, and hence belief is more necessary to such a people than to all others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: when a religion has struck its roots in a democracy, beware of disturbing it; watch it carefully as a precious bequest. Do not seek to supersede old religious opinions by new ones, because the transition may leave people temporarily without belief and vulnerable to physical gratifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments should act as if they believed in immortality
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole effectual means which governments can employ in order to have the doctrine of the immortality of the soul duly respected, is ever to act as if they believed in it themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical prescription: governments should display scrupulous conformity to religious morality in great affairs to teach the community to know, love, and observe it in lesser matters. Tocqueville rejects empowering clergy politically and prefers governmental moral example over official philosophies or state religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiritual improvement enhances material welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a closer tie than is commonly supposed between the improvement of the soul and the amelioration of what belongs to the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: elevating and enlarging the soul makes people more capable of succeeding in material undertakings; conversely, enervating the soul weakens capacities for both great and small purposes. Therefore moral/spiritual cultivation is instrumentally valuable for prosperity and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove objects of human actions to a distance in skeptical democratic ages
rubrics_metrics.description: In times marked by equality of conditions and sceptical opinions, it is important to remove to a distance the objects of human actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale and tactics: when faith in a future life fades, people tend to gratify immediate desires and give up protracted undertakings. Philosophers and those in power must teach the habit of conceiving and executing long-term projects, showing that protracted effort yields lasting results even in democratic, unstable societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must act with a view to the future and banish chance from politics
rubrics_metrics.description: The task of those in power is ... to act with a view to the future: by acting thus, the leading men of democracies not only make public affairs prosperous, but they also teach private individuals, by their example, the art of managing private concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific prescriptions: avoid sudden favor or undeserved promotion (which in democracies is especially pernicious), ensure that advancement appears to result from effort not chance, and practically teach that wealth, fame, and power are rewards of labor to restore love of the future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every advancement should appear the result of effort
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable that every advancement should there appear to be the result of some effort; so that no greatness should be of too easy acquirement, and that ambition should be obliged to fix its gaze long upon an object before it is gratified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: promotion and honors should be visibly tied to attainments and service, not to chance or fleeting popular favor, to cultivate patient ambition and long-term orientation among citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Among Americans all honest callings are honorable
rubrics_metrics.description: Amongst a democratic people, where there is no hereditary wealth, every man works to earn a living... The notion of labor is therefore presented to the mind on every side as the necessary, natural, and honest condition of human existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sociocultural effect: equality of conditions ennobles labor and collapses prior status distinctions between callings; remuneration and visible work give professions an air of resemblance so that 'every honest calling is honorable.' This is a positive civic norm to value work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy inclines people toward industrial and commercial callings
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all the tastes and habits which the equality of condition engenders naturally lead men to commercial and industrial occupations... Agriculture ... improves most slowly amongst democratic nations; commerce and manufactures attract those seeking quicker returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences and warning: democracy's spread of tastes for speedy prosperity encourages commerce and manufactures, producing rapid national industrialization but also exposure to systemic commercial panics because many are engaged in the same risky pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor narrows workmen and enlarges masters
rubrics_metrics.description: When a workman is unceasingly and exclusively engaged in the fabrication of one thing, he ultimately does his work with singular dexterity; but at the same time he loses the general faculty of applying his mind to the direction of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sociopolitical result: the more extensive the division of labor, the more the artisan is degraded intellectually while masters acquire broader administrative capacities; this dynamic entrenches social differences within manufacturing and weakens workers' mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactures can engender a new manufacturing aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion as the mass of the nation turns to democracy, that particular class which is engaged in manufactures becomes more aristocratic... Thus it would appear ... that aristocracy should naturally spring out of the bosom of democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative analysis: the manufacturing aristocracy differs from territorial aristocracy—it's confined, not permanently cohesive, and often harsh. Tocqueville warns friends of democracy to watch this development as a distinct channel by which inequality and aristocratic features may reemerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of conditions softens manners
rubrics_metrics.description: We perceive that for several ages social conditions have tended to equality, and we discover that in the course of the same period the manners of society have been softened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlative claim: Tocqueville treats equality and growing civility as linked facts, suggesting that social leveling produces milder manners. This functions as both an observation and a standard for assessing social change.
